title: Natchez MS Annual Events Calendar 2024
h1: Your Complete Guide to Natchez’s Year‑Round Events
meta_description: Discover every Natchez MS annual event on our 2024 calendar—festivals, parades, concerts, and more. Click for dates, tips, and local insights you won’t want to miss.
intro: Imagine strolling down Canal Street on a crisp spring morning, the scent of magnolia blossoms mixing with the distant echo of a marching band. That’s Natchez in a nutshell, and the rhythm of our town is set by the events that line the calendar year after year. From the thunderous fireworks over the bluff to the quiet charm of a historic reenactment at Emerald Mound, there’s always something pulling us out of the house and into the community. In this guide we’ll walk you through the must‑see festivals, the seasonal celebrations that draw locals and tourists alike, and the little‑known gatherings that keep the Miss‑Lou spirit alive. Grab a coffee, settle in, and let’s map out the Natchez MS annual events that define our town’s heartbeat.

sections.heading: Springtime in Natchez: Festivals, Flowers, and Family Fun
sections.body: When March rolls around, the city awakens with a burst of color that rivals the azaleas blooming along Main Street. The first big draw is the Natchez Spring Arts Festival, tucked into the historic downtown block between Canal and Main. Local artists set up easels outside Stanton Hall, and you can snag a watercolor of the bluff while your kids chase balloons near the riverfront. It’s not all polished; the food trucks line US‑61, serving everything from catfish po’boys to vegan tacos, and the lines can stretch, especially on Saturday afternoon. If you prefer a slower pace, the Natchez Garden Walk on the second Saturday offers guided tours of private gardens hidden behind wrought‑iron gates, a perfect excuse to see the historic homes in full bloom. The event is free, but parking on Liberty Rd can be a nightmare when the crowd peaks, so a short walk from the historic district is worth the trek. A highlight you shouldn’t miss is the annual Easter Egg Hunt at King's Tavern, where the historic tavern’s courtyard transforms into a wonderland for kids. The organizers hand out handcrafted eggs, and the prize for the fastest finder is a voucher for a free pastry at the tavern’s bakery. Expect a few families to dominate the hunt, but the atmosphere stays friendly and festive. By the end of April, the Natchez Spring River Run draws joggers and spectators alike, looping along the bluffs with the Mississippi River as a backdrop. The race is well‑organized, though the early morning start means you’ll need a warm jacket in case the river fog rolls in. The post‑race celebration at Under‑the‑Hill includes live blues, a perfect way to unwind after pounding the pavement. All these spring events share a common thread: they pull the community together while showcasing the natural beauty and historic charm that make Natchez unique.

sections.heading: Summer Celebrations: Music, Food, and Riverfront Revelry
sections.body: Summertime in Natchez feels like a perpetual block party, especially once the heat settles over the river and the townsfolk spill onto the streets. The crown jewel is the Natchez Summer Music Festival, a three‑day extravaganza that takes over the riverfront park and the historic district. Headliners perform on the stage at the bluff, while local bluegrass groups fill the alleys near the Old Courthouse. Tickets are reasonable, but the best spots fill up fast, so arriving early on Thursday night is a smart move. The festival’s food scene is a culinary tour of the South: you’ll find gumbo from a family‑run joint that’s been serving the riverboats for generations, and a pop‑up BBQ stand that claims to have the best hickory‑smoked ribs in the Miss‑Lou area. If you’re looking for a quieter evening, the weekly Sunset Concerts on the riverbank offer acoustic sets that blend perfectly with the rustle of the cottonwoods. Bring a blanket and a cooler; the vibe is relaxed, and the crowd is a mix of retirees, college students, and tourists who’ve driven up US‑61 just for the view. Mid‑July brings the Natchez Riverboat Parade, a dazzling procession of historic steamboats lit up like floating lanterns. The parade routes past the Natchez Visitor Center, and you can watch from the promenade on Canal Street or from a rented pontoon on the water. The boats are beautifully restored, but the ticket prices for the onboard dinner cruise can be steep, so it’s worth budgeting if you want the full experience. For families, the annual Natchez Summer Carnival at the fairgrounds is a must‑go. Rides, games, and a midway that feels like a throwback to the 1970s keep kids entertained, though the lines for the Ferris wheel can be long during peak hours. The carnival also hosts a nightly fireworks show over the river, a spectacle that draws crowds from across Louisiana and Arkansas. The summer calendar is packed, but the energy is infectious, and every event feels like a celebration of our river heritage and Southern hospitality.

sections.heading: Fall Festivities: Harvest, History, and Haunted Nights
sections.body: When the leaves turn amber along Liberty Rd, Natchez shifts into a slower, more reflective rhythm, yet the calendar stays lively with harvest festivals and historic reenactments that draw both locals and out‑of‑state visitors. The Natchez Harvest Festival kicks off the first weekend of October at the historic Emerald Mound site, where artisans display hand‑woven baskets, locally made jams, and pumpkin carvings that rival any county fair. The festival includes a corn maze that stretches across the mound’s fields; it’s a fun challenge, though the paths can be confusing after dark, so bring a flashlight. Live folk music fills the air, and you’ll hear fiddlers playing tunes that have been passed down through generations of river families. Food stalls serve up sweet potato pies and fried catfish, and the prices are fair, especially compared to downtown vendors. A standout event is the Natchez Ghost Walk, a guided nighttime tour that starts at the bluff and weaves through the haunted corners of St. Mary’s Catholic Church and the old jail on Main St. The guide tells stories of Civil War soldiers and 19th‑century scandals, and the fog that rolls in off the river adds an eerie ambience. It’s popular, so reservations are recommended; the walk can feel cramped if you show up without a spot. For history buffs, the annual Civil War Reenactment at the Natchez National Historical Park happens the second weekend of November. Volunteers in period uniforms recreate a skirmish that actually took place near the bluff, and the accuracy is impressive, though the crowd can be a bit touristy, with many taking selfies rather than listening to the narration. The park’s visitor center offers a quieter exhibit on the same day, perfect if you need a break from the bustle. Finally, the Thanksgiving Day Parade on Main St provides a small‑town twist on the big‑city tradition, featuring marching bands from nearby high schools, local fire trucks, and a float made entirely of corn husks. It’s a charming sight, though the parade route can cause traffic snarls on US‑61, so plan your drive accordingly. Fall events in Natchez blend agricultural pride, deep‑rooted history, and a touch of the supernatural, giving you a reason to visit the town even after the summer heat fades.

sections.heading: Winter Wonders: Holiday Lights, Parades, and Cozy Gatherings
sections.body: Winter in Natchez may be mild, but the town lights up with a festive spirit that rivals any major city, and the calendar is packed with events that keep the cold at bay. The season kicks off with the Natchez Christmas Parade on the first Saturday of December, rolling down Canal Street with floats adorned in twinkling lights, marching bands from the Natchez High School marching squad, and a horse‑drawn carriage carrying Santa himself. The parade draws crowds from as far as Baton Rouge, and parking on the bluff can be a headache, so many locals opt to walk from the downtown hotels. After the parade, the downtown square transforms into a holiday market where local craftspeople sell hand‑stitched quilts, wooden carvings, and homemade mulled cider. Prices are reasonable, and you can often haggle a bit with the vendors, especially if you’re buying a few items. The highlight of the winter calendar is the Natchez Holiday Lights Festival, a week‑long showcase of illuminated displays at historic homes like Stanton Hall and the Natchez Museum of African American History. The lights are professionally installed, creating a magical glow that reflects off the Mississippi River at night. Admission is modest, but the lines can be long on weekends, so a weekday visit gives you a more intimate experience. If you’re looking for a cozy indoor event, the annual Natchez Winter Jazz Series at King's Tavern offers intimate performances by regional musicians, paired with a menu of comfort food—think chicken pot pie and hot buttered bourbon. The tavern’s low‑ceilinged room amplifies the sound, making every note feel personal, though the space fills quickly, so a reservation is wise. For families, the Holiday Storytime at the Natchez Public Library on the second Saturday of December brings together local authors who read classic Christmas tales to kids, followed by a gingerbread decorating contest. The library’s historic reading room, with its original woodwork, adds a nostalgic charm, and the event is free, though you’ll need to sign up early because spots fill up fast. New Year’s Eve is celebrated with a riverfront fireworks display that launches from the bluff, lighting up the night sky over the Mississippi. The best viewing spots are the park benches along the riverwalk, but they’re a coveted commodity, so arrive early and bring a blanket. The winter schedule may be shorter, but each event feels thoughtfully curated, offering both communal celebration and intimate moments that keep Natchez’s heart warm through the chill.

faqs.q: When is the Natchez Spring Arts Festival and what can I expect?
faqs.a: The Natchez Spring Arts Festival usually runs the first weekend of March in the downtown block between Canal and Main. Expect local painters, live music, food trucks on US‑61, and a family‑friendly Easter Egg Hunt at King’s Tavern. Parking can be tight, so plan to walk or use a rideshare.

faqs.q: Where can I watch the Natchez Riverboat Parade?
faqs.a: The Riverboat Parade floats past the Natchez Visitor Center and lines the riverbank along Canal Street. You can watch from the promenade, a nearby park bench, or even from a rented pontoon on the river. Arrive early for a good spot; tickets for the onboard dinner cruise are optional but pricey.

faqs.q: What family activities are available during the Natchez Harvest Festival?
faqs.a: The Harvest Festival at Emerald Mound offers a corn maze, pumpkin carving contests, live folk music, and local food stalls with sweet potato pie and fried catfish. There’s also a kids’ craft area where they can make basket‑weaving projects under supervision.

faqs.q: How do I get tickets for the Natchez Holiday Lights Festival?
faqs.a: Tickets are sold online through the Natchez Tourism website and at the visitor center. Prices are modest—around $10 for adults—and you can buy a combo ticket that includes a guided tour of the illuminated historic homes. Weekday visits avoid the longest lines.

faqs.q: Is there a free holiday event for kids in Natchez?
faqs.a: Yes, the Natchez Public Library hosts a free Holiday Storytime on the second Saturday of December, featuring local authors, a gingerbread decorating contest, and a cozy reading of classic Christmas tales. Spots fill quickly, so register online ahead of time.
